topics.title: How to turn quadratics into parabolas easily
topics.text:
HOW TO GRAPH ANY QUADRATIC



Step 1 - Take the quadratic $y = ax^2 + bx + c$ or $x = ay^2 + by + c$



Step 2 - It turns into $y = a(x + \frac{b}{2a})^2 - (\frac{b^2 - 4ac}{4a})$

or $x = a(y + \frac{b}{2a})^2 - (\frac{b^2 - 4ac}{4a})$



Step 3 - Graph as a parabola, and enjoy!

If the diameters of the three inner circles are in a ratio of 1:2:3, what fraction of the largest circle is shaded? Express your answer as a common fraction. (Diagram 1st attachment).

3) It takes Avi one half-hour longer to make a basket than it takes Markus. After 28 hours, Markus has made one more basket than Avi has made. How many hours does it take Avi to make one basket?



4) Suppose N is a positive integer such that N − 1 is even, N − 2 is divisible by 3, N − 3 is divisible by 5, and N − 5 is divisible by 7. What is the least possible value of N?

Kayla then divides one of the existing piles into two new piles. She finds the product of the numbers of stones in the two new piles and adds it to the previous product. 15) Frankie the frog stands at the number 0 on a number line and wants to hop to the number 8. He can hop 1, 2 or 3 units forward in a single jump. How many different ways are there for Frankie to reach the number 8?



16) The median and the mean of the five integers 10, 12, 26, x, x are equal. What is the sum of all possible values of x?



17) What is the perimeter of a right triangle with an area of $10 cm^2$ and a hypotenuse of length 10 cm? Express your answer in simplest radical form.

topics.title: k Middle School Math FAQ
topics.text:
Hi! It looks like there are a few questions that get asked repeatedly on this forum in particular.  I figured it might be a good idea to combine all of these questions into one announcement post for future use.  I'm not sure whether these explanations are actually middle school level, but it's worth giving this a shot.



Why is it that $0.99\ldots = 1$?

Hidden for lengthI think the main issue people have with this is the concept of summing up infinitely many $9$s.  What does it mean to sum infinitely many terms?  Do we ever stop?



The answer?  We don't! The idea is not that we're summing infinitely many terms here.  It's rather that as we take more and more terms we get closer and closer to 1, so that it makes sense to say "as the number of terms approaches infinity, this sum approaches 1." We make this rigorous below.



Definition: Let $\{x_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ be an infinite sequence of real numbers. Define the sequence of partial sums $\{s_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ via \[s_n := x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_n.\]We say that the sequence of partial sums converges to a real number $L$ if the following holds: for all $\epsilon > 0$, there exists an $N\geq 0$ such that \[|s_n - L| < \epsilon\qquad\text{for all }n\geq N.\]In other words, after a certain point, all partial sums are within $\epsilon$ of $L$.



This definition makes more sense if you're thinking about it as a game. Imagine you're a little child who is being forced to clean your room. Your parents have a good idea of what they want the room to be in order for it to be considered clean.  (Maybe they want it perfectly clean, or maybe they're ok with a little bit of leeway.)  How can you, as the child, prove then that this room is actually up to their standards? We can't just pick some "closeness" parameter and expect that "if you're within the ideal scenario by this much then you're good to go". After all, if this closeness parameter is too large, then you got away with not cleaning your room!



Instead, the solution is to make the closeness parameter vary, in the sense that you can actually choose this parameter to be as small as you want it to. In this case, the mother can prove that you cleaned your room via the following algorithm. First, she chooses some real number $r$ to serve as a temporary closeness parameter. After this, you as the little boy need to pick a point in time for which you can say confidently "after this point of time, the difference between what you wanted and what I had was at most $r$!" This works much better than the previous case because despite the fact that the mother can make this $r$ as small as possible, you're still able to show her proof regardless. That's pretty convincing if you ask me! It also gets around the pesky paradox of asking what it actually means to sum up infinitely many terms of a series, for example: all we want is for the series to get close enough after some finite period of time.



With that, we can now formally state what it means for $0.99\cdots = 1$.



THEOREM. Set $x_n = 9\cdot 0.1^n$ for all $n\geq 1$, and define the sequence of partial sums $\{s_n\}$ as before. For example, \[s_1 = 0.9, \quad s_2 = 0.99,\quad \text{and}\quad s_3 = 0.999.\]Then the $s_n$ converge to $1$ as $n$ goes to infinity.



Proof. Let $\epsilon > 0$. Note that for any individual $k$, one may write \[s_k = x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_k = 9\cdot 0.1 + 9\cdot 0.1^2 + \cdots + 9\cdot 0.1^k = \dfrac{0.9(1-0.1^k)}{1-0.1} = 1 - 0.1^k.\]Now choose $k>0$ such that $0.1^k < \epsilon$. (Note that this is clearly possible, since $0.1^k$ gets arbitrarily small as $k$ gets large.) This means that \[|1 - s_k| = |1 - (1 - 0.1^k)| = 0.1^ k < \epsilon.\]Since $\epsilon$ was arbitrary, we win our little game, and so the $s_k$ get arbitrarily close to $1$ as desired.  $\blacksquare$



It's worth noting that there's skepticism in suggesting that we're summing up infinitely many terms to get a sum equal to $1$. And in that regard, this debate is valid! In fact, we never consider summing up infinitely many terms, because what does that even mean? The solution around this? Real analysis.




Why does $1+2+3+\cdots = -\tfrac{1}{12}$?

Hidden for lengthIt doesn't.



Longer answerThat being said, if we were to assign a real number value to this sum, then $-\tfrac{1}{12}$ would make the most sense.



The reason for this is because of something called the Zeta function. For all $s>1$, we can define the zeta function as \[\zeta(s)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty\dfrac1{n^s}=\dfrac1{1^s}+\dfrac1{2^s}+\dfrac1{3^s}+\cdots.\]For example, $\zeta(2)=\tfrac{\pi^2}6$. Of course, this is only defined for the positive $s$; how do we extend this definition to the negative and complex $s$? The existence of such an extension is based off the theory of analytic continuation.  What exactly is this type of continuation?  Unfortunately, this is rooted deep in complex analysis, and so the explanation below might be very very complicated, but I'll try to give it a shot, and if there are any confusing parts, respond in this thread and I or someone else will try to clarify.



Some of you may be familiar with the derivative of a function $f$ going from $\mathbb R$ to $\mathbb R$.  If you're not, let's just say it's defined as the function $f':\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, where for all $x$ in our domain, \[f'(x) = \lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}.\]As a simple example, for $f(x) = x^2$, compute \[\dfrac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h} = \dfrac{(x+h)^2 - x^2}{h} = \dfrac{2xh+h^2}{h} = 2x+h;\]it is thus clear that as $h\to 0$, this expression approaches $2x$, and so $f'(x) = 2x$ for all $x$.  (We have now an obvious question of whether this is always defined.  In general, this is not true, but let's just pretend that this wrinkle doesn't exist, since it does for most of the *nice* functions that we work with (e.g. polynomials) we generally work with.)



You may haven noticed that I made a bit of a fuss about the domain of the derivative: I said it had to go from $\mathbb R$ to $\mathbb R$.  But there's nothing stopping us from working in the complex numbers!  Indeed, the definition above makes complete sense even if $x$ and $h$ are complex numbers.  (Check this!  Nothing that we did above used explicitly the fact that $x$ and $h$ were real.)  Upon doing so, however, we gain a whole lot of power.



Let's think about this for a second.  In the real numbers, we only have two directions for where our $h$ can approach zero: from the left, and from the right.  This is actually not a very strong condition.  (For example, we can have functions defined on the real numbers which are differentiable but whose derivatives are not integrable.  In other words, the Fundamental Rule of Calculus does not always apply!)  But what happens when we move this to the complex numbers?  Now, we have two dimensions of $h$ to work with.  In effect, when we take the limit as $h\to 0$ in the complex plane, we make sure that this limit holds true regardless of the path that $h$ takes to get to the origin. This is an extremely powerful condition - for example, the function $f(z) = \overline{z}$ (complex conjugation) does not have a derivative everywhere!  It is so powerful, in fact, that we give a special name to functions which do have derivatives everywhere.



Definition: Let $R\subset\mathbb C$ be a subset of the complex numbers, and let $f:R\to\mathbb C$ be a complex-valued function.  We say $f$ is analytic if its derivative is defined everywhere in $R$.



We are now ready to start talking about this thing called an analytic continuation.  Unfortunately, I won't be able to do too much, since proving results like these requires some hefty complex analysis that is somewhat complicated (and that I don't actually know), so I will just be content in stating the results.



Definition: Let $f_1$ and $f_2$ be analytic functions on domains $\Omega_1$ and $\Omega_2$, respectively.  Suppose that $\Omega_1\cap\Omega_2$ is not empty and that $f_1=f_2$ on $\Omega_1\cap\Omega_2$.  Then $f_2$ is called an analytic continuation of $f_1$ to $\Omega_2$.



In other words, as long as our function $f_2$ agrees with $f_1$ somewhere, we can view $f_2$ as somehow extending $f_1$ to a region beyond just $\Omega_1$.



But so what?  All we've done is create some definition that may or may not be useful.  Why do we care?  Well, remember how I said that analytic functions were great things?  Now we see one of the reasons why.



Theorem:If it exists, then the analytic continuation of $f_1$ to $\Omega_2$ is unique.



This in effect means that there is only one way to extend $f_1$ past $\Omega_1$ onto $\Omega_2$.  This is a rather amazing and extremely powerful statement.  In particular, it says that knowing the value of a complex function in some subset of the complex numbers uniquely determines the function at every other point.



So how is this useful?  Well, go back to the zeta function $\zeta(s)$ from above.  As I said before, our definition of $\zeta(s)$ in terms of the sums of a bunch of terms is only defined, so to speak, for positive $s$.  (For negative $s$, this thing diverges, and for complex $s$, it's hard to tell.)  How do we extend this to negative and complex $s$?  The kicker, which you might have saw coming, is that



Fact: $\zeta(s)$ is analytic on $\mathbb R_{>1}$.



This means that we can use this analytic continuation stuff to figure out values of $\zeta(s)$ for negative and complex $s$!



It turns out this is done via the formula \[\zeta(s)=2^s\pi^{s-1}\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi s}2\right)\Gamma(1-s)\zeta(1-s).\]Here $\Gamma(\cdot)$ is the gamma function, which itself is an analytic continuation of the factorials. Although the details are sort of complicated, the one main thing you need to know is that \[\Gamma(n) = (n-1)!\]for all positive integers $n$.  Thus, we may write \begin{align*}\zeta(-1) &= 2^{-1}\pi^{-2}\sin\dfrac{-\pi}2\Gamma(2)\zeta(2) \\&= \dfrac12\cdot\dfrac{1}{\pi^2}\cdot (-1)\cdot1!\cdot\dfrac{\pi^2}{6} = \boxed{-\dfrac{1}{12}}.\end{align*}Thus, the whole "sum of positive integers equals $-\tfrac{1}{12}$" thing comes from the fact that one can "write" \[1+2+3+\cdots = \dfrac{1}{1^{-1}} + \dfrac{1}{2^{-1}} + \dfrac{1}{3^{-1}} + \cdots = \zeta(-1) = -\dfrac{1}{12}.\]

So although the normal zeta function doesn't make sense for negative numbers, we can extend the definition of this function through complex analysis to include something like $\zeta(-1)$. This is what "allows" expressions like $1+2+\cdots$ to have "defined" values.





If I missed any other common questions, or if the explanations above need clarification, let me know.

topics.text:
I had this problem:

Click to reveal hidden textFind the smallest positive k such $2^{39} + k$ is divisible by 63


and the solution:

Click to reveal hidden text$2^6 = 1 \pmod{63}$

$2^{36} = 1 \pmod{63}$

${2^{36}}{2^3} = 2^3 \pmod{63}$

$2^{39} = 8 \pmod{63}$

Hence the answer is $63-8=55$

topics.title: How to find the square root of irrational number
topics.text:
I had following question in the practice paper:



[quote]When $4+\sqrt{7}$ is presented in the form of perfect square it will be equal to:

(there were four options given)[/quote]



I quickly went on squaring each option, and finally in option (c), I found $\{(\frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{7}+1))\}^2=4+\sqrt{7}$ and it was correct. When I checked solutions, it solved it like this:



[quote]$4+\sqrt{7}$

$=\frac{8+2\sqrt{7}}{2}   ...\text{step (1)}$

$=\frac{(\sqrt{7})^2+1+2.\sqrt{7}.1}{2}$

$=\frac{(\sqrt{7}+1)^2}{(\sqrt{2})^2}$

$=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1+\sqrt{7})^2$

[/quote]

Somehow I feel step (1) is more sort of artificial or unintuitive or not so obvious. The whole solution looks like reverse engineering from the known solution which unfortunately we dont know beforehand in the exam.
